newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks end lower on renewed banking fears.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks end lower on renewed banking fears.

text.p: Japanese stocks met with a renewed wave of sales on Monday, with the key market index closing two percent lower.
Brokers said overall sentiment was dampened by reignited fears over the banking sectors' profitability.
The key 225-share Nikkei average shed 354.46 points or 2.00 percent to close at 17,334.90, after briefly dipping to 17,280.20. Its March futures finished 280 points lower at 17,380.
Sales of bank shares were triggered by a variety of vague rumours about new problems or possible derivatives losses in the banking industry, brokers said.

The rumours raised concern about whether banks already struggling to tackle bad loan problems will be able to survive in a more competitive environment when the government pushes through its "Big Bang" financial reforms.
"The bank shares' vulnerability to the rumours proved that few investors want to buy the shares now," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
The banking sector 0#BNK.T ranked as the top percentage loser on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

Turnover on the first section was relatively moderate at 348 million shares, little changed from Friday's 398 million shares. Declining issues exceeded gainers 918 to 186, while 151 issues were unchanged.
The broader-based TOPIX index lost 26.88 points or 1.99 percent to close at 1,326.60. The Nikkei 300 average dipped 5.18 points or 2.02 percent to end at 251.04.

Asked about vague rumours circulating in financial markets about possible derivatives losses within the banking industry, a Finance Ministry official told Reuters: "We have not heard any such rumours."

A spokesman for Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp denied that it had suffered any such loss. Its shares fell 150 yen to end at 1,100 yen, making it the second largest percentage loser on the first section.
Shares in Fuji Bank Ltd closed 120 yen lower at 1,180 yen, ranking as the seventh biggest loser.
Shares in Chuo Trust & Banking Co Ltd lost 68 yen to finish at 722 yen, while Yasuda Trust & Banking Co Ltd dipped 33 yen to end at 360 yen.
Daiwa Bank Ltd lost 32 yen to end at 477 yen.

Adding to the gloom was a mid-afternoon announcement by Moody's Investors Service that it had lowered its rating outlook for Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Yasuda Trust & Banking and Chuo Trust & Banking to negative from stable.
The prospect of fierce competition in the financial sector after "Big Bang" deregulation is also giving the market a negative undertone, brokers said.

Over the weekend, the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau director, Eisuke Sakakibara, said Japan's financial sector, especially banks, must be ready for major "bloodletting" after the planned "Big Bang" reforms.
In the declining sectors, banking was followed by sea transport, fisheries, mining and iron/steel.
There were no major advancing sectors.

Shares in Janome Sewing Machine Co Ltd shed 80 yen to close at 220 yen, hit by news that health concerns had forced some makers of "24-hour bath" systems to stop selling the product. Janome makes the baths, which ensure a hot tub of water around-the-clock, but was not among the firms which suspended sales pending a safety review.
Blue chips stood out against the overall gloom. Sony Corp rose 70 yen to 7,830 yen.
The second section index fell 6.66 points to 1,726.20. The over-the-counter (OTC) index was down 7.71 points at 1,213.71.
-- Hiroko Nakata, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-8027
